title: Switchboard deck insulation
plain: Is there good insulating matting in front of and behind the switchboards, with a voltage rating you can prove?
why: Wet, hot engine rooms make electric shock much more dangerous, so the floor around a switchboard must protect the person standing there.
checks: Matting at the front and rear of each switchboard
Matting complete, with no cuts, holes or gaps
Voltage rating suits the switchboard voltage
Marking or paper proof of the safe working voltage
ready: Matting certificate or rating mark that can be read
Drawings showing composite insulating deck, if you have no mats
Matting laid flat, clean and dry
Spare matting or a repair plan for damaged pieces
traps: No matting at the front or the rear
Matting torn, cracked or missing a section
Rating too low for a high voltage board
No mark or paper showing the rating
Mat curling up and creating a trip hazard
say: Both the front and rear of every switchboard have insulating matting, and we inspect it during our safety rounds. The rating is marked on the mat and we hold the certificate. Where a deck is composite insulating material, the drawings show the extent and the safe voltage.

practice.q: What voltage is this matting rated for?
a: Name the class or voltage from the mark or certificate
Say it suits the switchboard voltage
Higher voltage boards need a higher class

practice.q: Do the starter boxes need matting too?
a: No, only switchboards need it, front and rear
Individual starter boxes are not counted as switchboards

tip: Walk round the boards before the inspection and check every mat for cuts and curled edges. Find the rating mark now so you can show it quickly.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices

title: Switchboard earth monitoring
plain: Do engineers know how the insulation monitors work and their settings, and are the boards free of significant earth faults?
why: A single earth fault is invisible but a second one trips the system, and low insulation can also give someone a shock.
checks: Insulation monitor on each primary and secondary distribution board
Readings on the monitors
Alarm set point against company procedure
Test button operated to show it is working
Understanding of earth lamps if that is all you have
ready: Company procedure giving IMD set values for each voltage
Insulation readings near as high as possible, not below 5 megohms on 440 V
Not below 2 megohms on 220 V
Record of earth faults found and fixed
Working test device on each monitor
traps: No procedure with IMD settings for each voltage
Officer cannot show the alarm set point
Alarm setting changed to stop it sounding
440 V board reading under 5 megohms
220 V board reading under 2 megohms
Monitor not working or defective
A consumer such as a deepwell pump causing a constant earth fault
say: Our procedure gives the alarm setting for each voltage level, and I can show you the set point on this monitor. We test it with the test button and we investigate any low reading until it is back as close to infinity as possible. We do not accept a standing earth fault, even if a machine is known to cause it.

practice.q: What is the minimum you accept on the 440 V board?
a: Aim for as near infinity as possible
Not less than 5 megohms
220 V system: not less than 2 megohms

practice.q: Why does a single earth fault matter?
a: Insulated neutral system keeps running on one fault
A second fault makes a short circuit and trips the system
Find and fix the first one early

tip: Check the readings on every board during your rounds. If a known pump causes a fault, fix it and do not call it normal.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices

title: Entering the machinery space during UMS
plain: Do engineers and bridge officers know the company rules for entering an unattended engine room, including the dead man alarm?
why: A person alone in an unattended engine room who collapses may not be found in time.
checks: Company procedure for safe entry during UMS
Safe entry notice at the engine room entrance
Dead man alarm test records, if fitted
Engine room and bridge log entries of recent entries
Alarm start and activation time, if safe to try
ready: Entry rules posted at the normal engine room entrance
Dead man alarm test records with results
Engine and bridge log books showing UMS status and entries
Officers who can explain the procedure
Bridge officer who knows the entry rules
traps: Nobody informs the bridge before entering alone
No regular contact with the bridge when there is no dead man alarm
A rating sent alone to the engine room while unattended
Dead man alarm not tested or tests not recorded
Alarm takes longer than company procedure or over 30 minutes
Entry rules not posted at the entrance
Dead man alarm defective
say: Before anyone enters the unattended engine room we inform the bridge, say how long we will stay, and start the dead man alarm. Without that alarm we call the bridge at fixed short intervals. We test the alarm regularly and record the result, and no rating goes in alone.

practice.q: What do you do when you enter the engine room alone at night?
a: Inform the bridge on entering and leaving
Say how long you will stay
Start the dead man alarm if fitted, or call the bridge at agreed intervals

practice.q: Is the dead man alarm required by SOLAS?
a: No, it is not a SOLAS requirement
If fitted, it must be used, tested and recorded under our procedure

tip: Test the dead man alarm on a set day and time the delay with a stopwatch. Know that number because the inspector may ask you to start it.

title: Engineers' alarm
plain: Do engineers know how the engineers' alarm works, and is it in good order and tested regularly with records?
why: In an engine room emergency, the engineers' alarm is how help is called from the accommodation.
checks: Company procedure for operation and testing
Test records for the alarm
Officer can point out the alarm activation points
Alarm works from the control room or manoeuvring platform
ready: Procedure with a description of how it works
Regular test records
Known list of activation points in the engine room
Alarm audible in the engineers' accommodation
Engineers who know where to assemble when it sounds
traps: No company procedure for operating and testing it
Officer does not know the procedure
Officer cannot find the activation points
No test records or tests missed
Alarm defective in any way
say: Our procedure describes how the engineers' alarm works and how often we test it, and we record each test. I can show you the activation points in the engine room. On a UMS ship it also sounds if a machinery alarm is not acknowledged within a set time, and it may be linked to the dead man alarm.

practice.q: Where can you operate the engineers' alarm from?
a: Engine control room
Manoeuvring platform as appropriate
Show the activation points in the machinery space

practice.q: When does it sound automatically on a UMS ship?
a: If a machinery alarm is not acknowledged within a set time
That time is not more than 5 minutes
It may also sound if the dead man alarm is not reset

tip: Learn the activation point locations by walking them in order. Keep test records in one place so you can show them at once.

title: Machinery alarm
plain: Do engineers and bridge officers know how the machinery alarm works, and is it in good order and tested regularly with records?
why: On a UMS ship the machinery alarm is the early warning that something in the engine room needs action.
checks: Company procedure for operation and testing
Test records for the machinery alarm
Engine room panel and bridge panel functions
Alarms heard and seen in the engine room, bridge, public rooms and cabins
Test of the alarm if the terminal allows
ready: Procedure with operation description and test requirements
Regular test records
Working audible and visual alarms in all required places
Bridge officers who know the panel functions
Alarm printer and system showing the correct time and date
traps: No company procedure for operation and testing
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure
Engineer or bridge officer does not know the panel functions
No test records or tests overdue
Engine room buzzer not working
Bridge, public room or cabin alarm not fully working
Machinery alarm defective in any way
say: The machinery alarm gives audible and visual warning in the engine room, on the bridge, in public rooms and in the engineers' cabins. We test it as our procedure says and record the result. Every alarm is acknowledged and acted on, and any inhibited alarm follows our SMS.

practice.q: What do you do with an alarm you cannot clear?
a: Acknowledge and act on all alarms
Report it to the Chief Engineer
Any inhibit follows the SMS and the cause is fixed soon

practice.q: How often do you test bilge high level alarms?
a: At least once every watch
Also as part of pre-UMS checks
Other alarms follow the PMS

tip: Brief the OOW on what each lamp and buzzer on the bridge panel means. Check the printer clock at the start of every watch.

title: Watertight doors
plain: Do officers know the rules for operating, inspecting and testing watertight doors, and are the doors in good condition?
why: Watertight doors limit flooding and fire spread, and wrongly operated doors have killed people.
checks: Company procedure for operation, inspection and testing
Test and inspection records
Bridge indicator and control panel
Local and remote operation shown on a sliding door
A rating describes local operation
ready: Procedure and test records, with tests at every fire drill
Bridge panel showing open and closed correctly
Instructions for use posted at each door
Rubber gaskets in good order, no hydraulic leaks
Doors normally closed at sea marked not to be left open
traps: No company procedure
Rating cannot describe or show local operation
Gasket damaged, poor or missing
Hydraulic oil leaking from the door mechanism
Door will not close from the bridge, or local alarm and light fail
Manual or emergency operation does not work
No posted instructions at the door
Doors left in emergency close mode on the bridge
Bridge shows closed but the door is open, or the reverse
Not tested at every fire drill
say: Our procedure covers operation, inspection and testing, and we test the doors at every fire drill. Remote closing from the bridge gives the local alarm and light, and we can work each door by hand from both sides. Instructions are posted at the doors and the bridge panel is not left in emergency close mode.

practice.q: How often do you test the watertight doors?
a: At least at every fire drill
Records kept
Do not leave bridge panel in emergency close

practice.q: How do you open this door if power fails?
a: Use the hand operation at the door
It works from both sides
Instructions are posted beside the door

tip: Brief the ratings on local operation and never cross a moving door. Check the bridge panel against the actual state of each door during the test.

title: Gas welding and cutting equipment
plain: Is the gas cutting kit in good order, with oxygen and acetylene cylinders stored apart, ventilated and outside accommodation and engine room?
why: Oxygen and acetylene are a fire and explosion risk if cylinders, hoses or fittings are wrong.
checks: Cylinder storage location
Distribution piping and manifolds
Hoses, torches, regulators and flashback arrestors
Records of inspection and replacement of arrestors and regulators
PPE for cutting and welding
ready: Oxygen and acetylene stored in separate compartments
Cylinders upright, secured for quick release, caps on
Annual inspection of arrestors and regulators recorded
Replacement 5 years from manufacture or per maker
Hoses in good condition: red acetylene, blue oxygen
Clean PPE free of oil and grease
traps: Oxygen and acetylene stored together
Cylinder valve end down
Cylinders not secured, or not easy to release in a fire
Empty cylinders mixed with full ones
Storage poorly ventilated, hot, salty, or with ignition sources
No No Smoking sign
Cylinder valves or fittings with oil, grease or paint
Valve left open after work
No flashback arrestors or non-return valves
Bolted flanges or rubber hose in fixed piping
Propane used
Leaking hose repaired instead of cropped or replaced
No record of arrestor and regulator checks
say: Oxygen and acetylene are stored in separate, ventilated spaces outside the accommodation and engine room, upright and secured for quick release. We close the valves after work and keep the hoses out of the weather. Arrestors and regulators are inspected annually and replaced on schedule, with records.

practice.q: Where do you keep spare cylinders?
a: Separate compartments for oxygen and acetylene
Ventilated, away from heat and traffic, outside accommodation and engine room
Upright, secured, valve caps on

practice.q: What safety devices must be on the hoses?
a: Non-return valves next to the torch
Flashback arrestors at the low pressure side of regulators
Both ends for long hoses

tip: Check cylinder labels, not just colours, and note manufacture dates on arrestors and regulators.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices

title: Electric welding equipment
plain: Do engineers and ratings know the electric welding safety rules, are they posted, and is the equipment in good condition?
why: Electric welding can cause shock, burns and fire, and wrong earthing can put current through the ship's structure.
checks: Welding set, nameplate, cables and electrode holder
Local switching to cut current quickly
Safety precautions posted in the workshop
Officer and a fitter or rating asked about the precautions
Spare electrodes and screens
ready: Safety precautions posted in the workshop
Nameplate showing output: DC not over 70 V, AC not over 25 V
Cables undamaged and not spliced
Earth return cable long enough, clamp near the work
Electrode holder fully insulated, electrodes kept dry
Clean, dry PPE and welding screens
traps: Officer or rating does not know the precautions
Precautions not posted
Ship's structure used as the earth return
Earth clamp not near the work, or return cable too short
Cable worn, damaged or spliced
DC output over 70 V or AC output over 25 V
No quick cut-off switch
Electrode left in the holder
Holder not fully insulated
Spare electrodes damp
PPE missing or oily
say: The precautions are posted in the workshop and everyone doing welding has been briefed. We check cables and holder before each use, and the earth clamp goes next to the work with a return cable back to the machine. The set voltage is on the nameplate and we never use the hull as the return.

practice.q: What is the maximum output voltage?
a: DC from rectifiers and inverters: 70 V
AC from transformers: 25 V
Shown on the nameplate

practice.q: How do you earth the welding set?
a: Clamp next to the work site
Return cable goes directly back to the machine
Never use the ship's structure as return

tip: Take the electrode out of the holder every time you stop. Keep spare electrodes in a dry container.
refs: MCA Code of Safe Working Practices

title: Planned maintenance system (PMS)
plain: Do staff know how to use the planned maintenance system, and does it show accurate maintenance and spare parts records?
why: Equipment that is not maintained on time, or spares that are missing, can fail when you need them most.
checks: Company PMS procedure
Overdue and deferred tasks in the system
Critical equipment spares against minimum stock
One spare part found in the store with the right box and stock
A deck officer and a junior engineer show how they record a task
ready: PMS procedure and operating instructions
Overdue tasks cleared, or approved by shore
Deferrals with documented shore approval
Critical equipment and minimum spare stock marked
Defects linked between defect list and PMS tasks
Spare locations and counts matching the system
traps: No company procedure for the PMS
Responsible officer does not know the system or procedure
Junior officer cannot show how to record a task
Defect not moved between the PMS and defect list
Task overdue past its date or grace period without shore approval
Equipment needed for safe operation not in the PMS
Deferrals without shore approval
Critical spares not tagged with minimum stock
Stock below minimum
Spare not in the store place or count wrong
say: Our SMS says what is in the PMS, who is responsible and what grace period applies. Overdue and deferred jobs have shore approval. Critical spares have minimum stocks and I can show you any part in the store matching the system.

practice.q: What if a task cannot be done by its due date?
a: Follow the grace period in the procedure
Ask shore management to approve a deferral
Record the approval

practice.q: Show me the record of a task you did.
a: Find the task in the PMS
Show completion date and notes
Explain the equipment it covers

tip: Before the inspection, filter for overdue and deferred jobs and check the approvals. Count a few critical spares yourself.
refs: OCIMF Safety Critical Equipment and Spare Parts Guidance

title: Lube oil and hydraulic oil analysis
plain: Is the ship enrolled in an oil analysis programme, and is there a procedure to act on the results and trends?
why: Oil analysis shows wear and contamination early, so damage can be stopped before machinery fails.
checks: The oil analysis programme and which oils are covered
Reports for the previous two cycles
Whether each oil was sampled on time
Red or amber results and the follow-up
Maintenance records showing the advice was done
ready: Programme listing every oil and its frequency
Analysis reports for the last two cycles
Shore or lab recommendations for red or amber results
Records showing the fix was carried out
Procedure for acting on a bad result
traps: No routine sampling programme
Officer does not know the company procedure
An oil not landed for analysis on schedule
A critical (red) result in the last two cycles
No evidence recommended action was taken
say: We follow the oil analysis programme and land the samples on time for every oil it lists. When a report shows amber or red, we get advice from the lab or the office and we act on it. The records show what was done to bring the oil back.

practice.q: What did you do about this amber result?
a: Show the lab or office advice
Show the maintenance record of the action
Explain how you checked it afterwards

practice.q: Which oils are in the programme?
a: Name the ones declared, such as stern tube and main engine sump oil
State the sampling frequency for each

tip: Keep red and amber reports with the follow-up actions stapled together. Plan sample landing at the next convenient port.

title: Conventional bunkering operations
plain: Do the people involved in bunkering know the company procedure, and do records show bunkering was planned and done as required?
why: Bunkering spills are common, and they usually happen when the plan is weak or people are distracted.
checks: Company bunkering procedure and checklists
A recent bunker plan and its content
Signatures of understanding and approval
Records and checklists for the same operation
Ullage gas checks before, during and after
An engine room rating about their role
ready: Bunker plan with people and duties named
Plan signed by all involved and by Master and Chief Engineer
ISGOTT bunker checklists completed at every stage
Records that show which tank was loading at each time
Tank atmosphere checks recorded
Bunker staff with no other duties during bunkering
traps: No procedure requiring a bunker plan with set content
Missing checklists for any stage
No record-keeping procedure
Officer unfamiliar with planning or records
Rating does not know their duties
Atmosphere checks not taken or not recorded
Plan missing key information or personnel roles
Plan not signed by all, or not approved by Master and Chief Engineer
Records show the plan was not followed
Records too thin to rebuild the operation
say: Every bunkering has a written plan naming who does what, signed by all officers and approved by the Master and Chief Engineer. We use the checklists at every stage, record the tanks and gas checks, and keep the bunker team free of other tasks.

practice.q: What is in your bunker plan?
a: Tank space, maximum volumes, valve settings
Loading rates for start, bulk and topping off
Communications, emergency stop and manning
Spill containment and who does what

practice.q: Who signs the plan?
a: All officers involved sign for understanding
Master and Chief Engineer sign for approval

tip: Use the same plan form for every operation and file the completed checklists with it so the full story is in one place.

title: Bunker fuel sampling and analysis
plain: Do engineers know the sampling and analysis procedure, and do records show samples were taken, kept or analysed?
why: Bad or non-compliant fuel can damage engines and break MARPOL Annex VI rules.
checks: Company procedure for fuel samples and analysis
Bunker delivery notes for the last twelve months
Analysis reports for the last twelve months
Samples retained for each delivery
Advisory notes in reports acted on
Oil Record Book Part 1 entries
ready: Procedure covering sampling, retention, analysis and problems
Delivery note for every bunkering
MARPOL sample retained for each delivery
Analysis for every residual fuel delivery
Distillate analysis frequency defined
Evidence advice from reports was followed
Oil Record Book Part 1 matching bunkering
traps: No procedure for samples, analysis and fuel quality problems
Officer does not know the procedure
Missing delivery note for a delivery
Sample not retained
No rule to analyse every residual fuel
No guidance on distillate analysis frequency
Analysis not done as procedure or contractor requires
Report advice not followed
say: Each bunkering gets a delivery note and a retained representative sample, and residual fuel goes for analysis every time. If the report raises a concern or we must use fuel early, we follow our procedure and contact the office. Delivery notes and analysis reports for at least the last twelve months are on board.

practice.q: What do you do if analysis shows off-spec fuel?
a: Follow the company procedure
Report to the office
Follow the advisory notes in the report

practice.q: What can you show for the last bunkering?
a: Delivery note and retained sample
Analysis report
Oil Record Book entry

tip: Keep delivery notes, analysis reports and sample labels in one folder sorted by date.

title: Fuel changeover procedures
plain: Do senior engineers know the fuel changeover procedures, and do records show changeovers followed the procedure and MARPOL?
why: A poorly done changeover can cause a blackout or loss of propulsion, or break the sulphur rules.
checks: Company and ship-specific changeover procedures
Records of a recent changeover
Vessel position during the changeover
Log entries made for entering and leaving an ECA
ready: Procedures for main engines, generators and boilers
Risk assessment behind the procedure
Changeover calculator and checklist
Log with volume of low sulphur fuel, date, time and position
Defined places and conditions where changeover may happen
traps: No company procedure for fuel changeover
No ship-specific procedure
Officer unfamiliar with either
Records missing or inaccurate
No log entry of volume, date, time and position for ECA entry or exit
Changeover done where the company said not to
Operating in breach of MARPOL Annex VI
say: We have a ship-specific changeover procedure based on risk assessment, with a calculator and checklist. We do changeovers in safe waters away from traffic, and log the volumes, date, time and position when entering or leaving an ECA.

practice.q: What must you log for an ECA changeover?
a: Volume of low sulphur fuel in each tank
Date, time and position
On completion before entry, and on start after exit

practice.q: Where do you not change over fuel?
a: Where risk of blackout or propulsion loss is high
Follow the company limits on location and traffic

tip: Start the changeover calculation early and time it with margin before the ECA boundary.

title: LNG fuel tank water-spray system
plain: Do officers know the LNG fuel tank water-spray system and how to run it, and is it inspected and maintained?
why: The deck water spray cools the LNG fuel tank and stops a fire from spreading if something goes wrong.
checks: Remote controls for the water-spray system and the posted instructions
Valve and control marking and settings
Piping, especially underneath, for corrosion and patching
A sample of nozzles for clogging
Isolating and stop valves turning freely
Maintenance plan and inspection records
ready: Operating instructions posted at the control station
Controls clear of obstruction and clearly marked
Maintenance plan that includes the water-spray system
Records of weekly, monthly, annual and five-year tasks as set out in the plan
Nozzles clean and not overpainted
Officer who can start the pumps and find the valves and drain point
traps: Instructions not posted at the control station
Officer does not know location, purpose or operation
Access to controls blocked
Valves or controls not marked or set correctly
Stop or isolating valves stiff or unmarked
Clogged or overpainted nozzles
Hard rust or temporary repairs on the pipework
No maintenance plan, or the system is not in it
Records incomplete or tasks recorded but not done
say: I can show you the remote controls, start the pumps and explain what each isolating and stop valve does. The instructions are posted here. Our maintenance plan covers flushing, cleaning filters and checking nozzles, and the records match what you can see on deck.

practice.q: How do you start the water-spray system?
a: Go to the remote control position
Start the pump and open the system valves as posted
Check flow at the nozzles

practice.q: Where is the drain point for the deck piping?
a: Show the drain location on deck
Say why it is drained
Know the isolating valve positions

tip: Run the system with fresh water in the planned test and look at every nozzle. Keep paint brushes away from the nozzles.

title: LNG bunkering ESD system
plain: Do the people on LNG bunkering know the bunkering emergency shutdown functions, and are they in good order, tested and maintained?
why: If something goes wrong during LNG transfer, the ESD must stop flow quickly and safely, and people must know how to trigger it.
checks: Company procedure for operating, inspecting, maintaining and testing the ESD
Pre-bunkering ESD test checklist from the last bunkering
Bunker station and remote control station panels and the fuel piping diagram
Override rules
An engineer and a rating asked about ESD purpose and manual controls
ready: Procedure covering functions, ESD failure and ship-shore link unavailable
Completed pre-arrival ESD test checklist
Inspection, maintenance and test records
Fuel handling manual describing the ESD
Fuel system diagram at the bunker station and remote station
Override only with documented Master authority
traps: Officers not familiar with the bunkering ESD
Instruments or controls at the bunker station not working
No fuel system diagram posted
No fuel handling manual, or it does not describe the ESD
No record of tests before bunkering
Records incomplete or maintenance not done
Rating does not know the manual ESD location or when to use it
ESD link not available and no contingency plan
ESD overridden without Master authorisation
System defective
say: The ESD stops the transfer in a controlled way and the ship-shore link lets either side shut it down. We test it before every bunkering and keep the checklist. I can show the manual controls, and an override needs the Master's documented authority.

practice.q: What happens when the ESD is activated?
a: Transfer stops in a controlled way
Manifold valves shut and pumps or compressors stop
Stage 2 can decouple the transfer system

practice.q: What if the ESD ship-shore link is not available?
a: Follow the contingency plan in the procedure
Do not start until the plan is satisfied

tip: Walk the rating through the manual ESD points before each bunkering, not just the officers.

title: LNG bunkering procedures
plain: Do the people involved know the company LNG bunkering procedures, and do records show bunkering was planned and carried out as required?
why: LNG is very cold and volatile, so a poor plan or missed checks can lead to leaks, fire or structural damage.
checks: Company LNG bunkering procedures and the fuel handling manual
A recent bunker transfer plan
Checklists (ISO or IAPH) used consistently
Records of tank pressures, temperatures and rates
An officer or rating about their role in the plan
ready: Detailed transfer plan with roles, limits, rates and emergency actions
Plan signed by all officers and approved by Master and Chief Engineer
Safety checklist signed by both persons in charge
Calculations of temperature, volume and vapour pressure
Stop and restart conditions in the plan
Pre-bunkering verification documented
traps: Procedure missing a required item, such as ESD description or ship side protection
No suitable checklists
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure
No suitable fuel handling manual
Person with a role does not know their duties
Plan missing key information or roles, or not fully signed
Records show the plan was not followed or are too thin
Checklists not completed, or ISO and IAPH mixed
No calculations of temperature, volume and vapour pressure
Checklist not signed by both PICs
No stop and restart conditions
Pre-bunkering verification not done and documented
say: Each LNG bunkering has a detailed plan with roles, limits, rates and emergency actions, signed by everyone and approved by the Master and Chief Engineer. We use one checklist set from start to finish, do the pre-bunkering verification, and record pressures, temperatures and rates.

practice.q: What do you verify before bunkering?
a: All communications including ship-shore link
Fixed and portable gas detection and fire detection
Remote controlled valves
Hose and coupling condition

practice.q: Can you switch between ISO and IAPH checklists?
a: No, use one set from pre-operation to completion
Both parties and the authorities must agree to use IAPH

tip: Pick the checklist set before the operation starts and keep it for the whole transfer.

title: LNG bunkering control station and manifold
plain: Are the safety measures at the LNG bunkering control station and manifold area in good condition?
why: A cold LNG leak can crack the steel deck, so the manifold needs protection and the control point must work from a safe place.
checks: Bunkering control location in a safe area
Controls and instruments there
CCTV of the manifold, or a manifold watch
Protection against cold damage at the manifold
Access limits, fire signs and PPE
ready: Controls for the shutdown valve and water-spray valves working
Tank pressure, temperature and level indicators working
Overfill alarm, auto shutdown, ventilation and gas alarms working
Insulated drip tray with drain valve, and water curtain or deck cover
Signs restricting the area to essential staff
PPE for cryogenic hazards
traps: Control location not in a safe area
Remote controls or instruments not working
CCTV fitted but not working or not used
No protection of the deck against brittle fracture
No insulated drip tray where leaks may happen
Water curtain not working or not used
Manifold area not marked for essential people only
No fire safety signs at access points
People at the manifold without suitable PPE
say: We run the bunkering from the control station in a safe area, where the shutdown and water-spray controls and the tank readings are working. At the manifold we have an insulated drip tray, water curtain and deck protection. Only essential people go there and they wear cryogenic PPE.

practice.q: How is the deck protected from an LNG leak?
a: Water curtain on the hull
Insulated drip tray with a drain valve
Cover for deck plating

practice.q: What do you watch from the control station?
a: Tank pressure, temperature and level
Overfill alarm and automatic shutdown
Gas and ventilation alarms around the lines

tip: Check CCTV and the drip tray drain before each bunkering, and have the PPE laid out in advance.

title: Remote fuel and lube oil valve controls
plain: Do officers know the remote fuel and lube oil valve controls, pump shut-offs and quick closing valves, and do they work?
why: In a machinery space fire you must cut off the fuel and oil from outside the space.
checks: Company procedure for inspection, testing and maintenance
Remote controls and pump shut-offs shown on the fire control plan
Quick closing valves armed and not tied open
Marking and access to controls
Maintenance plan and records
ready: Procedure with frequency and method of tests
Controls clearly marked with what they control
Access to controls clear
Quick closing valves armed, not secured open
Maintenance plan listing these items
Complete test records
traps: No company procedure
Controls not clearly marked
Access to controls blocked
Quick closing valve not armed
Quick closing valve secured open by wire, rope or similar
Officer does not know purpose, location or operation
Plan does not include these items or all tests
Records incomplete or work recorded but not done
Any control defective
say: The remote controls and pump stops are outside the machinery space, marked and unobstructed, and shown on the fire control plan. The tank quick closing valves are armed and never secured open. We test them as per our maintenance plan and the records are complete.

practice.q: Why are the controls outside the engine room?
a: So they are not cut off by a fire in the space
SOLAS requires it for fuel tank valves and pump stops

practice.q: What is wrong if a quick closing valve is wedged open?
a: It cannot close in a fire
It must be armed and free to close

tip: Walk all the controls on the fire control plan at the interval in your maintenance plan and check the marking and the trip wires.

title: Fire prevention in machinery spaces: hot surfaces and oil spray
plain: Do officers know how to stop oil spraying onto hot surfaces in the engine room, and are the protections inspected and maintained?
why: Most engine room fires start when oil meets a hot surface or other ignition source.
checks: Company procedure and the ship-specific inspection checklist
Records of periodic inspections

say: Our procedure gives the alarm set point, the actions on alarm and the test frequency. The oil mist alarm is set at not more than 5 percent of LEL, we calibrate sensors as the maker requires, and I can test it for you.

practice.q: What is the maximum alarm set point?
a: Not more than 5% of the lower explosive limit
About 2.5 mg/l of oil mist in air

Keep steam heating on continuously in ice waters
Check the heating works before entering
